question: What was life expectancy at birth for males and for females in Mali in 2019?

question: According to the timeline of 75 years of public health, in which year did WHO found the Expanded Programme on Immunization?
answer: According to the timeline of 75 years of public health, WHO founded the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1974 [who-whs-2023-p088-fig3.3].

Figure 3.3 Seventy-five years of improving public health, 1948–2023
[Text layer in figure] Figure 3.3 Seventy-five years of improving public health, 1948–2023 1948 WHO Constituion comes into force 1974 WHO founds the Expanded Programme on Immunization to bring Following an ambitious 12-year global vaccination campaign led by WHO, smallpox is eradicated 1999 The ﬁrst global strategy for the prevention and control of NCDs 2000 The WHO Global Outbreak Alert Framework Convention on Tobacco Control • WHO launches the "3 by 5" initiative, which aims to bring treatment to 3 million people living with HIV by 2005 and lays the groundwork for reaching 13 Child Growth Standards are launched to help every child grow in an equitable way 2012 The World Health Assembly adopts WHO's implementation plan on maternal, infant, and young child nutrition 2014 The Every Newborn Action Plan is endorsed by the World Health Assembly 2015 All United Nations Member States adopt the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development 2019 UN Declaration on UHC 2020 Access to COVID-19 Tools Accelerator 2022 Agreement for cooperation on the health of humans, animals, plants and the environment 2021 More than 74 million lives had been saved through tuberculosis (TB) Ref. (5)
[Vision description] **Type of figure:** Timeline infographic (S-curved path depicting public health milestones from 1948 to 2023).

**Data values (Year: Event details):**

* **1948:** WHO Constitution comes into force
* **1974:** WHO founds the Expanded Programme on Immunization to bring life-saving vaccines to all the world's children
* **1978:** 
  * WHO launches the global diarrhoeal diseases programme with oral rehydration salts at its heart
  * The International Conference on Primary Health Care, in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan, sets the aspirational goal, "Health for All", laying the groundwork for WHO's call for UHC
* **1980:** Following an ambitious 12-year global vaccination campaign led by WHO, smallpox is eradicated
* **1988:** The Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI), is launched
* **1999:** The first global strategy for the prevention and control of NCDs
* **2000:** The WHO Global Outbreak Alert and Response Network (GOARN) is established to detect and combat the international spread of outbreaks
* **2003:** 
  * The World Health Assembly unanimously adopts WHO's first global public health treaty, the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control
  * WHO launches the "3 by 5" initiative, which aims to bring treatment to 3 million people living with HIV by 2005 and lays the groundwork for reaching 13 million people infected with HIV with ART by 2013
* **2004:** WHO co-established the UN Road Safety Collaboration to prevent road traffic injuries
* **2005:** The International Health Regulations are revised
* **2006:** WHO Child Growth Standards are launched to help every child grow in an equitable way
* **2012:** The World Health Assembly adopts WHO's implementation plan on maternal, infant, and young child nutrition
* **2014:** The Every Newborn Action Plan is endorsed by the World Health Assembly
* **2015:** All United Nations Member States adopt the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development
* **2019:** UN Declaration on UHC
* **2020:** Access to COVID-19 Tools Accelerator
* **2021:** 
  * More than 74 million lives had been saved through tuberculosis (TB) prevention, diagnosis and treatment since 2000
  * HIV treatment coverage expanded rapidly with well over 17 million people living with HIV on ART by the end of 2015
* **2022:** Agreement for cooperation on the health of humans, animals, plants and the environment
* **2023:** WHO's 75th anniversary

**Main trends:** The graphic displays chronological milestones in WHO's 75-year history, starting from its constitution in 1948 and ending with its 75th anniversary in 2023.

Working closely with Member States and other partners, WHO has seen many remarkable milestones achieved during its 75 years of existence. Smallpox was eradicated in 1980 after an ambitious 12-year global vaccination campaign led by WHO. By 2023, five of the six WHO Regions were certified free of wild poliovirus and two of the three wild poliovirus strains have been globally eradicated (6). HIV treatment coverage has expanded rapidly with over 28.7 million people living with HIV on ART by the end of 2021 – up from 7.8 million in 2010 (7). More than 74 million lives have been saved through TB prevention, diagnosis and treatment since 2000 (8), 42 countries have eliminated malaria (9) and 47 countries have eliminated at least one NTD (10). Moreover, in the past two decades, tobacco use has dropped by a third (11), maternal mortality has fallen by a third and child mortality has halved (12,13).
Building on past achievements to prepare for the next stage of global health

9. World malaria report 2022. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2022 (https://apps.who.int/iris/handle/10665/365169, accessed 22 April 2023).
10. Global report on neglected tropical diseases 2023. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023 (https://apps.who.int/iris/ handle/10665/365729, accessed 22 April 2023).

Working closely with Member States and other partners, WHO has seen many remarkable milestones achieved during its 75 years of existence. Smallpox was eradicated in 1980 after an ambitious 12-year global vaccination campaign led by WHO. By 2023, five of the six WHO Regions were certified free of wild poliovirus and two of the three wild poliovirus strains have been globally eradicated (6). HIV treatment coverage has expanded rapidly with over 28.7 million people living with HIV on ART by the end of 2021 – up from 7.8 million in 2010 (7). More than 74 million lives have been saved through TB prevention, diagnosis and treatment since 2000 (8), 42 countries have eliminated malaria (9) and 47 countries have eliminated at least one NTD (10). Moreover, in the past two decades, tobacco use has dropped by a third (11), maternal mortality has fallen by a third and child mortality has halved (12,13).

question: What was the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) of the global under-five mortality rate in 2000-2010 and in 2010-2021?
answer: The average annual rate of reduction (ARR) of the global under-five mortality rate (U5MR) was 4.0% during the first period (2000–2009) and fell to 2.7% during the second period (2010–2021) [who-whs-2023-p018-text-002] [who-whs-2023-p019-fig1.4].

events.query: global under-five mortality rate average annual rate of reduction 2000 2010 2021

results.text: Globally, NMR declined at a slower rate compared to U5MR, and both declined more slowly during the second decade (2010–2021) compared to the first decade (2000–2009). The ARR of the NMR dropped from 3.2% during 2000–2009 to 2.2% during 2010–2021, while the ARR of U5MR fell from 4.0% during the first period to 2.7% during the second period (Figure 1.4). This slowdown has been particularly pronounced since the start of the SDG era in 2015.

Source: Ref. (4).
[Vision description] This is a line chart titled "Figure 1.4 Trends in the global under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, 2000–2021".

The y-axis represents "Mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" ranging from 0 to 80.
The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021, with labels at 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2021.
The chart background is divided into two shaded regions: a green-shaded region from 2000 to 2010, and a red-shaded region from 2010 to 2021.

There are two lines in the chart:
- A light blue line represents "U5MR" (under-five mortality rate).
- A purple line represents "NMR" (neonatal mortality rate).

Data values and trends:
For U5MR (light blue line):
- In the 2000-2010 period (green-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 4.0%.
- In the 2010-2021 period (red-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 2.7%.
The U5MR shows a continuous decrease from approximately 78 per 1000 live births in 2000 to approximately 38 per 1000 live births in 2021.

For NMR (purple line):
- In the 2000-2010 period (green-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 3.2%.
- In the 2010-2021 period (red-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 2.2%.
The NMR shows a continuous decrease from approximately 30 per 1000 live births in 2000 to approximately 18 per 1000 live births in 2021.

Overall trends:
Both U5MR and NMR show a decreasing trend from 2000 to 2021.
The rate of reduction for both U5MR and NMR was higher in the 2000-2010 period compared to the 2010-2021 period.
U5MR is consistently higher than NMR throughout the entire period.

Substantial global progress has been made in reducing child mortality since 2000. Approximately 10 million (9.9 million, UI: 9.8–10.1 million)2 children under 5 years of age died globally in 2000, corresponding to an under-five mortality rate (U5MR) of 76 (UI: 75–78) deaths per 1000 live births. Both the global number of deaths and the U5MR halved by 2021 (Figure 1.4). However, 5.0 million (UI: 4.8–5.6 million) children in 2021 tragically died before reaching their fifth birthday. Just under half (47%) of these deaths – about 2.3 million (UI: 2.2–2.6 million) – occurred during the first month of life. The global neonatal mortality rate (NMR) stood at 18 (UI: 17–19) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, a 43% drop from 31 (UI: 30–32) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000. The global U5MR in 2021 was 38 (UI: 36–42) deaths per 1000 live births (4).

The chart is divided into two main stacked sections:
1.  "Neonatal deaths (0–28 days)" at the bottom.
2.  "Post-neonatal under-five deaths (1–59 months)" on top of the neonatal deaths.

Each of these two sections is further subdivided by WHO region, represented by different colors in the legend:
*   African Region (red)

*   Region of the Americas (light blue)

The chart shows a clear downward trend in both neonatal deaths and post-neonatal under-five deaths from 2000 to 2021.

In 2000, the total global under-five deaths were approximately 10 million. By 2021, this figure had decreased to approximately 5 million.

For neonatal deaths (0–28 days):
*   In 2000, the total was approximately 3.5 million.
*   In 2021, the total was approximately 2.2 million.
The African Region and South-East Asia Region contribute the largest proportions to neonatal deaths throughout the period.

For post-neonatal under-five deaths (1–59 months):
*   In 2000, the total was approximately 6.5 million.
*   In 2021, the total was approximately 2.8 million.
The African Region and South-East Asia Region also contribute the largest proportions to post-neonatal under-five deaths.

The overall trend for both categories and all regions is a decrease in deaths over the 21-year period. The African Region consistently shows the largest number of deaths in both categories.

Children around the world face vastly different chances of survival depending on where they are born. While U5MR in the African Region fell by 52% between 2000 and 2021, it remained the highest at 72 (UI: 65–84) deaths per 1000 live births – almost twice the global U5MR and about nine times higher that of the European Region which was eight (UI: 7–8) deaths per 1000 live births. Despite a 34% drop in NMR from 40 (UI: 39–42) deaths per 1000 live births in 2000 to 27 (UI: 24–31) deaths per 1000 live births in 2021, the number of neonatal deaths in the African Region remained stubbornly high at about 1.1 million annually since 2000 (Figure 1.5), owing to the increasing number of live births. The South-East Asia Region saw a big decline in deaths as the number of neonatal and post-neonatal under-five deaths dropped by 65% and 78%, respectively, between 2000 and 2021.

[Vision description] **Type of figure:** 
Clustered vertical bar chart titled "Figure 2.13 Proportion of population using WASH services, globally and by WHO region, 2020". 
- **Y-axis:** "Proportion of the population (%)" ranging from 0 to 100 in increments of 20.
- **X-axis:** WHO regions and global summary: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.
- **Legend categories:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services (blue)
  - Safely-managed sanitation services (green)
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water (purple)

**Printed Data Values (by region/series):**

* **African Region:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: 32%
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 23%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: 28%

* **Region of the Americas:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: 81%

* **Eastern Mediterranean Region:**

* **European Region:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: 92%
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 70%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: not labelled (bar missing)

* **South-East Asia Region:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: not labelled (bar missing)
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 46%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: 71%

* **Western Pacific Region:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: not labelled (bar missing)
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 65%

* **Global:**
  - Safely-managed drinking-water services: 74%
  - Safely-managed sanitation services: 54%
  - Hand-washing facility with soap and water: 71%

**Main comparisons and trends:**
- **Highest values:** European Region has the highest coverage for safely-managed drinking-water services (92%) and safely-managed sanitation services (70%). Eastern Mediterranean Region tied with Region of the Americas for highest hand-washing facilities (81%).
- **Lowest values:** African Region has the lowest proportion across all three categories (32% drinking water, 23% sanitation, 28% hand-washing).
- **Missing data:** Several regions lack complete aggregate data for all three WASH services (indicated by missing bars).

Despite progress, WASH services are still not universally available. Safely managed drinking-water services – i.e. located on premises, available when needed and free from contamination – were accessible by 74% of the global population in 2020, leaving 2 billion people with only basic or limited services or having to rely on unprotected drinking-water sources. Only slightly over half (54%) of the global population were using safely managed sanitation services, with excreta safely disposed on-site or treated off-site. Around 3 in 10 (29%) people worldwide lacked a basic handwashing facility with water and soap at home (37). The coverage of WASH services varies across WHO regions (Figure 2.13), as well as across and within countries.

Notably, global life expectancy at birth increased from 46.5 years in 1950 to approximately 73.0 years in 2019 and, despite the setback caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, it is projected to reach 77.0 years by WHO’s 100th anniversary in 2048 (1,2).1 WHO regions such as Eastern Mediterranean, South-East Asia and Western Pacific – where resources were scarcer and life expectancy was relatively lower in 1950 – have observed the greatest gains, seeing increases in life expectancy of over 30 years between 1950 and 2019. However, progress was slower in WHO’s African Region, which had the second lowest life expectancy at 37.6 years in 1950 but became the region with the lowest life expectancy in 2019 at under 65 years. Nonetheless, the absolute gain in Africa was still greater than that in the Americas where life expectancy increased from 56.0 years in 1950 by about 21 years to 77.2 years in 2019. An estimated 287 000 (UI: 273 000–343 000) women lost their lives due to largely preventable causes related to pregnancy and childbirth in 2020 – approximately 800 women every day – equivalent to 223 (UI: 202–255) deaths per 100 000 live births that year.

The maternal mortality ratio levels, as well as the rates of progress and slowdown, have been uneven across WHO regions (Figure 1.1). The WHO South-East Asia Region maintained the fastest reduction rate during the MDG era and the first five years of the SDG era, reducing the maternal mortality ratio from 372 (UI: 336–423) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2000 to 117 (UI: 106–133) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2020. The Region of the Americas, the Western Pacific Region and the European Region saw a trend reversal, with the maternal mortality ratio levels increasing
between 2016 and 2020 after having decreased during the MDG era. However, the levels of the maternal mortality ratio have remained low (below 100 deaths per 100 000 maternal deaths) since 2000.

Notably, global life expectancy at birth increased from 46.5 years in 1950 to approximately 73.0 years in 2019 and, despite the setback caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, it is projected to reach 77.0 years by WHO’s 100th anniversary in 2048 (1,2).1 WHO regions such as Eastern Mediterranean, South-East Asia and Western Pacific – where resources were scarcer and life expectancy was relatively lower in 1950 – have observed the greatest gains, seeing increases in life expectancy of over 30 years between 1950 and 2019. However, progress was slower in WHO’s African Region, which had the second lowest life expectancy at 37.6 years in 1950 but became the region with the lowest life expectancy in 2019 at under 65 years. Nonetheless, the absolute gain in Africa was still greater than that in the Americas where life expectancy increased from 56.0 years in 1950 by about 21 years to 77.2 years in 2019. In contrast, Europe had the highest life expectancy at birth (61.3 years) in 1950 and made the most modest gain of about 17 years by 2019.

The maternal mortality ratio levels, as well as the rates of progress and slowdown, have been uneven across WHO regions (Figure 1.1). The WHO South-East Asia Region maintained the fastest reduction rate during the MDG era and the first five years of the SDG era, reducing the maternal mortality ratio from 372 (UI: 336–423) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2000 to 117 (UI: 106–133) deaths per 100 000 live births in 2020. The African Region, while keeping the ARR relatively stable at 2.0% for the past two decades, continued to have the highest maternal mortality ratio. The Region of the Americas, the Western Pacific Region and the European Region saw a trend reversal, with the maternal mortality ratio levels increasing
between 2016 and 2020 after having decreased during the MDG era. However, the levels of the maternal mortality ratio have remained low (below 100 deaths per 100 000 maternal deaths) since 2000.

The highest maternal mortality ratios (≥1000, dark red) are concentrated in Central Africa, including countries like Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan, and Somalia. Other countries in this category include Afghanistan and Yemen.

The lowest maternal mortality ratios (<20, very light pink) are observed across North America (Canada, United States), most of Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and parts of East Asia (e.g., Japan, South Korea). Many countries in South America also show lower ratios, generally in the 20–99 or 100–299 range.

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland, Western Sahara, and some parts of Central Asia. "Not applicable" (grey) is shown for areas like the Arctic.

[Vision description] **Type and Structure**
Figure 2.7 consists of two line charts side by side, showing global data for children under 5 years of age from 2000 to 2022. Both charts feature horizontal x-axes labeled with years (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2022).

* **Left Chart:** Shows "Prevalence (%)" on the vertical axis (scaled 0 to 40). 
* **Right Chart:** Shows "Number (millions)" on the vertical axis (scaled 0 to 250).
* **Legend:** Categories include Stunting (yellow/orange line), Overweight (blue line), Wasting (red point/error bar), and 95% confidence interval (shaded band/error bar).

**Data Values**

*Prevalence (%) of children under 5 years affected:*
* Stunting: 2000 = 33.0%; 2022 = 22.3%
* Overweight: 2000 = 5.3%; 2022 = 5.6%
* Wasting: 2022 = 6.8% (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

*Number (millions) of children under 5 years affected:*
* Stunting: 2000 = 204.2 million; 2005 = 197.1 million; 2010 = 184.8 million; 2015 = 169.1 million; 2022 = 148.1 million
* Overweight: 2000 = 33.0 million; 2005 = 35.5 million; 2010 = 36.2 million; 2015 = 38.0 million; 2022 = 37.0 million
* Wasting: 2022 = 45.0 million (2000–2015 values are not labeled)

**Main Trends and Comparisons**
* **Stunting:** Decreased steadily between 2000 and 2022 in both prevalence (from 33.0% to 22.3%) and total numbers (from 204.2 million to 148.1 million). It remains the highest category among the three conditions throughout the period.
* **Overweight:** Remained relatively stable in prevalence, slightly rising from 5.3% in 2000 to 5.6% in 2022. The total number increased from 33.0 million in 2000 to a peak labeled value of 38.0 million in 2015, before slightly dropping to 37.0 million in 2022.
* **Wasting:** Data is only labeled for 2022, standing at a prevalence of 6.8% and affecting 45.0 million children.

Still, in 2022, there were 49.8 million children under 5 years of age affected by stunting in the South-East Asia Region [30.1% (UI: 28.3–32.0)], 56.2 million in the African Region [31.0% (UI: 30.2–31.8)] and 22.9 million in the Eastern Mediterranean Region [25.1% (UI: 23.4–26.8)].
Globally, an estimated 148.1 million children under 5 years of age were affected by stunting in 2022. These numbers may become substantially higher as the global food and nutrition crisis continues to unfold – fueled by conflict, climate change and the enduring effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The full impact of the crisis on stunting may take years to manifest (27).

Stunting
Stunting is the result of chronic and recurrent malnutrition in mothers and in children who do not grow to their maximum potential.
The global prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years of age fell from 33.0% (UI: 32.4–33.5) in 2000 to 22.3% (UI: 21.8–22.9) in 2022. The decline occurred more rapidly during the MDG era, with an ARR of 2.0% between 2000 and 2015 – spurred by the rapid decline during the second half of the period – compared to the decline since the start of the SDG era in 2015, with an ARR of 1.4%.
Stunting prevalence also declined in all WHO regions, albeit at different paces (Figure 2.8). In both the European and the Western Pacific regions, prevalence fell by more than half between 2000 and 2022, but the progress slowed in the
Western Pacific Region in the more recent period. In contrast, prevalence reduction has gathered speed in the South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean regions in the second half of the MDG era.

Still, in 2022, there were 49.8 million children under 5 years of age affected by stunting in the South-East Asia Region [30.1% (UI: 28.3–32.0)], 56.2 million in the African Region [31.0% (UI: 30.2–31.8)] and 22.9 million in the Eastern Mediterranean Region [25.1% (UI: 23.4–26.8)].
Globally, an estimated 148.1 million children under 5 years of age were affected by stunting in 2022. These numbers may become substantially higher as the global food and nutrition crisis continues to unfold – fueled by conflict, climate change and the enduring effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The full impact of the crisis on stunting may take years to manifest (27).

[who-whs-2023-p058-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 58]
Stunting
Stunting is the result of chronic and recurrent malnutrition in mothers and in children who do not grow to their maximum potential.
The global prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years of age fell from 33.0% (UI: 32.4–33.5) in 2000 to 22.3% (UI: 21.8–22.9) in 2022. The decline occurred more rapidly during the MDG era, with an ARR of 2.0% between 2000 and 2015 – spurred by the rapid decline during the second half of the period – compared to the decline since the start of the SDG era in 2015, with an ARR of 1.4%.
Stunting prevalence also declined in all WHO regions, albeit at different paces (Figure 2.8). In both the European and the Western Pacific regions, prevalence fell by more than half between 2000 and 2022, but the progress slowed in the
Western Pacific Region in the more recent period. In contrast, prevalence reduction has gathered speed in the South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean regions in the second half of the MDG era.

Still, in 2022, there were 49.8 million children under 5 years of age affected by stunting in the South-East Asia Region [30.1% (UI: 28.3–32.0)], 56.2 million in the African Region [31.0% (UI: 30.2–31.8)] and 22.9 million in the Eastern Mediterranean Region [25.1% (UI: 23.4–26.8)].
Globally, an estimated 148.1 million children under 5 years of age were affected by stunting in 2022. These numbers may become substantially higher as the global food and nutrition crisis continues to unfold – fueled by conflict, climate change and the enduring effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. The full impact of the crisis on stunting may take years to manifest (27).

[who-whs-2023-p058-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 58]
Stunting
Stunting is the result of chronic and recurrent malnutrition in mothers and in children who do not grow to their maximum potential.
The global prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years of age fell from 33.0% (UI: 32.4–33.5) in 2000 to 22.3% (UI: 21.8–22.9) in 2022. The decline occurred more rapidly during the MDG era, with an ARR of 2.0% between 2000 and 2015 – spurred by the rapid decline during the second half of the period – compared to the decline since the start of the SDG era in 2015, with an ARR of 1.4%.
Stunting prevalence also declined in all WHO regions, albeit at different paces (Figure 2.8). In both the European and the Western Pacific regions, prevalence fell by more than half between 2000 and 2022, but the progress slowed in the
Western Pacific Region in the more recent period. In contrast, prevalence reduction has gathered speed in the South-East Asia and Eastern Mediterranean regions in the second half of the MDG era.

question: How did the global age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use change between 2000 and 2020?
answer: Between 2000 and 2020, the global age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older declined by over 30%, decreasing from 32.7% in 2000 to 22.3% in 2020 [who-whs-2023-p024-text-000].

**Main comparisons and trends:**
*   For "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female", the prevalence of tobacco use decreased in all WHO regions and globally from 2000 to 2020.
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Both sexes" was in the South-East Asia Region (50.4%), and the lowest was in the African Region (17.9%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Male" was in the South-East Asia Region (68.2%), and the lowest was in the African Region (28.7%).
*   The highest prevalence in 2000 for "Female" was in the South-East Asia Region (32.5%), and the lowest was in the African Region (7.1%) and Western Pacific Region (5.0%).
*   In all regions and globally, male prevalence of tobacco use was significantly higher than female prevalence in both 2000 and 2020.

The age-standardized current tobacco use prevalence was higher among men than among women across the world. The male-to-female ratio at global level was 4.7 in 2020, rising from 3.0 in 2000 and indicating a slower reduction among men compared to women. The lack of progress among men in relative terms was observed in all WHO regions, except for Europe where the ratio dropped slightly from over 2 in 2000 to 1.9 in 2020 – a level that was lowest among all six WHO regions. The ratio remained highest in Western Pacific Region throughout the two decades, rising from 10.2 in 2000 to 16.6 in 2020.

The Global Action Plan for Prevention and Control of NCDs has set a target to reduce the current tobacco use prevalence by 30% between 2010 and 2025. question: Was anaemia prevalence higher among pregnant or non-pregnant women aged 15-49, and what were the values?
answer: Anaemia prevalence was higher among pregnant women [36.5% (UI: 34.0–39.1)] than among non-pregnant women [29.6% (UI: 26.6–32.5)] [who-whs-2023-p060-text-001].

events.query: anaemia prevalence pregnant non-pregnant women 15-49

results.text:
Although the global prevalence of anaemia in women aged 15–49 years decreased slightly from 2000 [31.2% (UI: 28.7–34.1)] to 2019 [29.9% (UI: 27.0–32.8)], the total number affected increased considerably due to population growth – from 492.9 million in 2000 to 570.8 million in 2019. Prevalence was higher among pregnant women [36.5% (UI: 34.0–39.1)] than non-pregnant women [29.6% UI: 26.6–32.5)]. Globally, the prevalence of mild anaemia increased slightly from 15.5% (UI: 14.2–17.3) in 2000 to 16.2% (UI: 14.9–17.6) in 2019, while moderate anaemia declined slightly from 14.1% (UI: 12.4–16.1) in 2000 to 12.7% (UI: 10.6–14.8) in 2019, as did severe anaemia
from 1.7% (UI: 1.4–2.0) in 2000 to 1% (UI: 0.8–1.4) in 2019, indicating a shift towards mild anaemia (Figure 2.9) (28).

A
range of thematic areas in health are addressed in the
SDGs and GPW 13. This chapter presents a summary
status of indicators included in both frameworks, organized
around the areas of infectious diseases, nutrition, injury and
violence, environmental risks, and UHC and health systems.
•2.1 Infectious diseases
Infectious diseases are primarily reflected in SDG target 3.3 which includes the indicators for HIV, TB, malaria, viral hepatitis and NTDs. This section summarizes the current status of these indicators as well as the GPW 13 indicators on AMR and poliomyelitis caused by wild poliovirus (WPV).
HIV

Poliomyelitis caused by WPV
Poliomyelitis is a highly infectious viral disease that primarily affects children under 5 years of age. WPV cases have decreased by over 99% since the launch of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative in 1988 – from an estimated 350 000 cases in more than 125 endemic countries to six reported cases in 2021 (24).
Of the three strains of WPV (types 1, 2 and 3), type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 was declared eradicated in 2019. Only type 1 WPV remains. In 2022, 20 WPV type 1 cases were reported in Pakistan, two cases in Afghanistan and eight cases in Mozambique (25).
Interrupting transmission of WPV1 and circulating vaccinederived poliovirus type 2 is the primary goal on the path to global polio eradication (26).

Legend categories are: Region of the Americas (light blue), Eastern Mediterranean Region (green), European Region (orange), South-East Asia Region (purple), Western Pacific Region (yellow), and Global (dark purple).

Trends:
*   Global (dark purple line) shows a consistent decrease from approximately 0.48 in 2000 to about 0.26 in 2021.
*   South-East Asia Region (purple line) shows a decrease from approximately 0.28 in 2000 to about 0.08 in 2021.
*   Region of the Americas (light blue line) shows a relatively stable trend, starting around 0.22 in 2000 and ending around 0.18 in 2021.
*   European Region (orange line) shows an initial decrease, then an increase from around 2007, ending around 0.18 in 2021.
*   Eastern Mediterranean Region (green line) and Western Pacific Region (yellow line) show the lowest rates, both remaining below 0.1 throughout the period, with the Western Pacific Region slightly higher than the Eastern Mediterranean Region.

Panel b. WHO African Region, eastern and southern Africa, western and central Africa and global.
The y-axis represents new HIV infections (per 1000 uninfected population), ranging from 0 to 6.0. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021.
Legend categories are: African Region (red), Eastern and southern Africa (light green), Western and central Africa (yellow), and Global (purple).

Trends:
*   Eastern and southern Africa (light green line) shows the highest rates, decreasing significantly from approximately 5.9 in 2000 to about 1.6 in 2021.
*   African Region (red line) shows a decrease from approximately 3.2 in 2000 to about 0.9 in 2021.
*   Western and central Africa (yellow line) shows a decrease from approximately 1.4 in 2000 to about 0.5 in 2021.
*   Global (purple line) shows the lowest rates in this panel, decreasing from approximately 0.5 in 2000 to about 0.26 in 2021.

Overall, all regions and global trends show a decrease in new HIV infections from 2000 to 2021, with African regions having significantly higher rates compared to other WHO regions.

results.text:
Working closely with Member States and other partners, WHO has seen many remarkable milestones achieved during its 75 years of existence. Smallpox was eradicated in 1980 after an ambitious 12-year global vaccination campaign led by WHO. By 2023, five of the six WHO Regions were certified free of wild poliovirus and two of the three wild poliovirus strains have been globally eradicated (6). HIV treatment coverage has expanded rapidly with over 28.7 million people living with HIV on ART by the end of 2021 – up from 7.8 million in 2010 (7). More than 74 million lives have been saved through TB prevention, diagnosis and treatment since 2000 (8), 42 countries have eliminated malaria (9) and 47 countries have eliminated at least one NTD (10). Moreover, in the past two decades, tobacco use has dropped by a third (11), maternal mortality has fallen by a third and child mortality has halved (12,13).
Building on past achievements to prepare for the next stage of global health

•2.1 Infectious diseases
Infectious diseases are primarily reflected in SDG target 3.3 which includes the indicators for HIV, TB, malaria, viral hepatitis and NTDs. This section summarizes the current status of these indicators as well as the GPW 13 indicators on AMR and poliomyelitis caused by wild poliovirus (WPV).
HIV

[who-whs-2023-p056-text-000 | 9789240074323-eng.pdf | page 56]
Poliomyelitis caused by WPV
Poliomyelitis is a highly infectious viral disease that primarily affects children under 5 years of age. WPV cases have decreased by over 99% since the launch of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative in 1988 – from an estimated 350 000 cases in more than 125 endemic countries to six reported cases in 2021 (24).
Of the three strains of WPV (types 1, 2 and 3), type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 was declared eradicated in 2019. Only type 1 WPV remains. In 2022, 20 WPV type 1 cases were reported in Pakistan, two cases in Afghanistan and eight cases in Mozambique (25).
Interrupting transmission of WPV1 and circulating vaccinederived poliovirus type 2 is the primary goal on the path to global polio eradication (26).

*   Global (dark purple line) shows a consistent decrease from approximately 0.48 in 2000 to about 0.26 in 2021.

Trends:
*   Eastern and southern Africa (light green line) shows the highest rates, decreasing significantly from approximately 5.9 in 2000 to about 1.6 in 2021.
*   African Region (red line) shows a decrease from approximately 3.2 in 2000 to about 0.9 in 2021.
*   Western and central Africa (yellow line) shows a decrease from approximately 1.4 in 2000 to about 0.5 in 2021.
*   Global (purple line) shows the lowest rates in this panel, decreasing from approximately 0.5 in 2000 to about 0.26 in 2021.

Figure 1.9 Age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older, WHO regions and global, 2000–2020
[Text layer in figure] Figure 1.9 Age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older, WHO regions and global, 2000–2020 2000 2020 African Region Region of the Americas Eastern Mediterranean Region European Region South-East Asia Region Western Paciﬁc Region Global Female 0 20 10 50 40 30 60 70 Male 0 20 10 50 40 30 60 70 Both sexes 0 20 10 50 40 30 60 70 Prevalence (%) 7.1 2.8 20.6 11.3 10.2 4.2 22.6 17.4 32.5 11.3 5.0 2.8 16.2 7.8 2000 2020 2000 2020 2000 2020 2000 2020 2000 2020 2000 2020 17.9 10.3 28.0 16.3 27.2 18.6 34.6 25.3 50.4 29.0 27.9 24.6 32.7 22.3 28.7 17.8 35.5 21.3 44.1 33.0 46.5 32.9 68.2 46.6 50.8 46.4 49.3 36.7 Source: Ref. (9).
[Vision description] This is a grouped bar chart showing the age-standardized prevalence of current tobacco use among persons aged 15 years or older, by WHO regions and globally, for the years 2000 and 2020.

The chart has three panels, stacked vertically, representing "Both sexes", "Male", and "Female".
The y-axis for all panels is "Prevalence (%)", ranging from 0 to 70 in increments of 10.
The x-axis for each panel shows different WHO regions: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.
Within each region/global category, there are two bars: a blue bar representing the year 2000 and an orange bar representing the year 2020.

Data values are as follows:

**Both sexes:**
*   **African Region:** 2000: 17.9%, 2020: 10.3%
*   **Region of the Americas:** 2000: 28.0%, 2020: 16.3%
*   **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** 2000: 27.2%, 2020: 18.6%
*   **European Region:** 2000: 34.6%, 2020: 25.3%
*   **South-East Asia Region:** 2000: 50.4%, 2020: 29.0%
*   **Western Pacific Region:** 2000: 27.9%, 2020: 24.6%
*   **Global:** 2000: 32.7%, 2020: 22.3%

**Male:**
*   **African Region:** 2000: 28.7%, 2020: 17.8%
*   **Region of the Americas:** 2000: 35.5%, 2020: 21.3%
*   **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** 2000: 44.1%, 2020: 33.0%
*   **European Region:** 2000: 46.5%, 2020: 32.9%
*   **South-East Asia Region:** 2000: 68.2%, 2020: 46.6%
*   **Western Pacific Region:** 2000: 50.8%, 2020: 46.4%
*   **Global:** 2000: 49.3%, 2020: 36.7%

**Female:**
*   **African Region:** 2000: 7.1%, 2020: 2.8%
*   **Region of the Americas:** 2000: 20.6%, 2020: 11.3%
*   **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** 2000: 10.2%, 2020: 4.2%
*   **European Region:** 2000: 22.6%, 2020: 17.4%
*   **South-East Asia Region:** 2000: 32.5%, 2020: 11.3%
*   **Western Pacific Region:** 2000: 5.0%, 2020: 2.8%
*   **Global:** 2000: 16.2%, 2020: 7.8%

**Main comparisons and trends:**
